title: JOSEPH CALLED ADULTERY “A GREAT WICKEDNESS AND SIN AGAINST GOD” BEFORE HE RAN — AND WHAT HAPPENED NEXT WILL CONFRONT EVERY CHRISTIAN WHO THINKS SECRET SIN HAS NO CONSEQUENCES
paragraphs: JOSEPH CALLED ADULTERY “A GREAT WICKEDNESS AND SIN AGAINST GOD” BEFORE HE RAN — AND WHAT HAPPENED NEXT WILL CONFRONT EVERY CHRISTIAN WHO THINKS SECRET SIN HAS NO CONSEQUENCES

He was young, far from home, betrayed by his own brothers, and alone with a woman who wanted him. Nobody from his family was watching. Nobody was coming to rescue him. But Joseph understood something our generation desperately needs to remember: the greatest danger was not getting caught. It was sinning against the God who had never abandoned him.
There is a moment in a person's life when everything they claim to believe is tested.
Not inside a church.
Not while worship music is playing.
Not while holding a Bible where everyone can see.
But behind a closed door.

When the phone is unlocked. When the conversation becomes inappropriate. When the message arrives that should never have been sent. When loneliness begins negotiating with conviction. When temptation whispers that nobody will ever find out.
And suddenly, the question is no longer whether you know what the Bible says.
The question is whether you love God enough to obey Him when disobedience seems easier.
Joseph knew that moment.
And what makes his story so disturbing, so beautiful, and so painfully relevant is that he did the right thing...
And still ended up in prison.
Read that again.
He refused sexual sin, honored his master, remained faithful to God, and lost his freedom because of a lie.
If you have ever wondered why obedience sometimes seems to cost more than compromise, stay with this story.
Because Genesis 39 is not simply about a young man resisting an immoral woman.
It is about what happens when a person decides that God's holiness matters more than personal pleasure, human approval, professional advancement, or even freedom.
And ultimately, it points us toward someone greater than Joseph.
Someone who faced temptation without surrendering.
Someone falsely accused and condemned.
Someone who suffered though He had committed no sin.
Someone whose name is Jesus Christ.
But before we reach the grace, we need to walk through the scandal.
Joseph did not arrive in Egypt as an ambitious young man pursuing a promising career.
He arrived as property.
His own brothers had betrayed him. The people who should have protected him had sold him. His father was grieving a son he believed was dead.
Imagine being carried into a foreign country with no certainty that you would ever see home again.
Imagine hearing unfamiliar voices, seeing unfamiliar faces, and realizing that the people who sold you were going home while you were being taken farther away.
Joseph had every human reason to become bitter.
He could have decided that integrity was pointless.
He could have argued that God had allowed too much suffering to expect obedience from him.
But Genesis 39:2 records a remarkable truth:
“And the LORD was with Joseph.” (KJV)
Not Joseph was comfortable.
Not Joseph was free.
Not Joseph understood everything.
The LORD was with Joseph.
The Hebrew text says:
וַיְהִי יְהוָה אֶת־יוֹסֵף
Vayehi Adonai et-Yosef.

A faithful rendering is, “And the LORD was with Joseph.” The Hebrew consonants יהוה represent God's covenant name, commonly rendered LORD in English Bibles; Adonai is the traditional Jewish spoken substitute.
That little word “with” changes everything.
God's presence was not proof that Joseph would never suffer.
God's presence meant suffering would not have the final authority over Joseph's life.
Somebody reading this needs to understand that.
You may be in a season you never chose.
You may have been betrayed by someone you trusted.
You may be carrying wounds that nobody in your church knows about.
You may have prayed faithfully and still watched your circumstances become worse.
Do not measure God's faithfulness only by the comfort of your surroundings.
Joseph was enslaved, yet the LORD was with him.
And the same God who sustained Joseph has not become incapable of sustaining His people today.
Joseph eventually served in the household of Potiphar, an Egyptian officer of Pharaoh. God prospered the work entrusted to Joseph, and Potiphar recognized that the LORD was with him.
Joseph gained responsibility.
Trust.
Access.
Influence.
Then the temptation came.
Genesis 39:7 says Potiphar's wife “cast her eyes upon Joseph” and said, “Lie with me.” (KJV)
There was nothing ambiguous about the proposition.
She wanted a sexual relationship with a man who was not her husband.
And Joseph was not dealing with an ordinary situation between two people of equal standing.
He was enslaved in her household. She belonged to the family that controlled his circumstances. Her position gave her power that Joseph did not possess.
The passage does not tell us everything Joseph felt. It does not say he was attracted to her, nor does it describe his private emotional struggle.
We should not invent what Scripture does not reveal.
But Scripture tells us what he chose.
He refused.
And the words he spoke are among the most courageous declarations of moral conviction in the Old Testament.
“How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?” — Genesis 39:9 (KJV)
Look carefully at what Joseph did not say.
He did not say, “What if my master finds out?”
He did not say, “What if this ruins my reputation?”
He did not say, “What if somebody sees us?”
His concern reached deeper.
“How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?”
The original Hebrew is even more striking.
וְאֵיךְ אֶעֱשֶׂה הָרָעָה הַגְּדֹלָה הַזֹּאת וְחָטָאתִי לֵאלֹהִים
Ve'eikh e'eseh hara'ah hagedolah hazzot vechatati l'Elohim?
Literally, the sense is:
“And how could I do this great evil and sin against God?”

The Hebrew word רָעָה (ra'ah) refers here to evil or wrongdoing. הַגְּדֹלָה (hagedolah) means “the great,” emphasizing the seriousness of the act. The expression וְחָטָאתִי לֵאלֹהִים (vechatati l'Elohim) means “and sin against God.”
Joseph was not describing a harmless attraction.
He was identifying the proposed act as grave moral evil.
And that matters because our generation has become extraordinarily skilled at renaming sin until it sounds less offensive.
Adultery becomes “finding happiness.”
Lust becomes “having needs.”
Deception becomes “protecting someone's feelings.”
Secret relationships become “emotional connections.”
Pornography becomes “private entertainment.”
And repentance is sometimes replaced with the comforting idea that God understands everything, so nothing needs to change.
Yes, God understands our weakness.
But His understanding does not transform evil into good.
Grace does not require God to abandon His holiness.
And love does not require Him to pretend that sin cannot destroy what He created to be beautiful.
Joseph understood that adultery would be a betrayal of Potiphar's trust, a violation of the marriage covenant, and ultimately an offense against God.
Genesis 39:9 also records Joseph acknowledging that Potiphar had withheld only his wife from him because she was married to him.
This was not simply a question of whether Joseph could obtain something he desired.
It was a question of whether he would violate a relationship God intended to be honored.
Long before the written Law of Moses was given to Israel, Joseph recognized the moral gravity of adultery.
And centuries later, Jesus would reveal that God's concern reaches beyond outward acts into the desires of the heart.
In Matthew 5:27–28, Jesus teaches that lustful intent itself violates the heart of the commandment against adultery.
That should confront every one of us.
Because some people have never physically committed adultery but have been secretly cultivating desires that dishonor their spouse.
Some have never met the person they are emotionally entangled with, yet they are giving that person affection, secrecy, and attention that belong within their marriage.
Some have convinced themselves that deleting the conversation means erasing the sin.
Others are unmarried but have begun treating people as objects for pleasure rather than neighbors bearing God's image.
And some are carrying profound shame over sexual sins they have already committed.
If that is you, please do not stop reading.
This story is not being told so that you will conclude you are beyond redemption.
It is being told because sin is serious, and the mercy of Jesus Christ is greater than your ability to repair yourself.
But mercy must never become permission to continue destroying what God calls us to surrender.
There is another detail in Joseph's story that deserves our attention.
Genesis 39:10 says that Potiphar's wife spoke to Joseph “day by day.”
Day by day.
Not one unexpected encounter.
Not one isolated invitation.
Repeated pressure.
Repeated opportunity.
Repeated refusal.
And Joseph did not merely refuse to sleep with her. The verse says he would not listen to her “to lie by her, or to be with her.” (KJV)
He was resisting the act and avoiding the compromising proximity.
That is a lesson many Christians desperately need.
You cannot consistently nourish temptation and then be surprised when resisting it becomes harder.
You cannot deliberately cultivate intimacy with someone else's spouse and assume your intentions will remain innocent.
You cannot keep returning to the same secret conversation, the same explicit content, the same dangerous setting, while insisting that you are simply testing your spiritual strength.
There are temptations we must confront by standing firm.
And there are temptations we must confront by getting away.
Joseph did both.
Then came the day that changed everything.
Genesis 39:11–12 describes Joseph entering the house to attend to his work. None of the men of the household were inside.
Potiphar's wife seized him by his garment and demanded that he lie with her.
This was no longer merely a verbal proposition.
She physically grabbed him.
And Joseph ran.
He left the garment in her hand and fled outside.
The Hebrew of Genesis 39:12 says:
וַיָּנָס וַיֵּצֵא הַחוּצָה
Vayyanas vayyetse hachutzah.
“And he fled and went outside.”
No extended negotiation.
No attempt to prove how strong he was by remaining in danger.
He escaped.

We must also recognize something important: Joseph was the person being sexually pressured and physically seized. The responsibility for that wrongdoing belonged to the woman who pursued and grabbed him.
The lesson is not that victims of coercion are guilty if they cannot escape.
The lesson is that Joseph, when he had the opportunity, refused to participate in wrongdoing and fled from the person violating his boundaries.
Sometimes the holiest thing you can do is leave.
Leave the conversation.
End the secret relationship.
Close the browser.
Block the contact.
Step away from the compromising situation.
Tell the truth to someone trustworthy.
Seek help before another decision deepens the damage.
The New Testament reinforces this principle.
“Flee fornication.” — 1 Corinthians 6:18 (KJV)
The Greek begins:
Φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν
Pheugete tēn porneian.
The verb φεύγετε (pheugete) is a present imperative meaning “flee” or “keep fleeing.” The noun πορνεία (porneia) refers broadly to sexual immorality.
Paul was not telling believers to become experts at standing as close to sexual sin as possible without crossing a technical boundary.
He commanded them to flee it.
Not because their bodies are worthless.
But because their bodies matter to God.
In the same chapter, Paul reminds Christians that they belong to Christ and are called to glorify God in their bodies.
That is why holiness is not merely a collection of restrictions.
It is the fitting response of someone redeemed by a Savior who gave Himself for them.
But here is the part of Joseph's story that many people would rather skip.
Joseph ran from sin.
And the consequences were terrible.
Potiphar's wife used the garment Joseph left behind as the centerpiece of a false accusation.
The very thing he abandoned while escaping became evidence she used against him.
Joseph was innocent of the alleged offense.
Yet he was imprisoned.
Can you imagine the questions that might arise in such a situation?
Why did doing the right thing lead to suffering?
Why was the liar believed?
Why did integrity not protect him?
Why did God not immediately expose the truth?
Scripture does not record Joseph asking those particular questions, so we should not place imaginary speeches into his mouth.
But the injustice itself is unmistakable.
And anyone who has ever been falsely accused, misunderstood, betrayed, or punished for doing what is right can recognize the pain of that reality.
Sometimes obedience costs you something.
Sometimes telling the truth damages your popularity.
Sometimes ending a sinful relationship leaves you lonely.
Sometimes refusing corruption closes a professional door.
Sometimes your commitment to Christ will be misunderstood by people who benefited from your compromise.
And sometimes doing what is right does not immediately make life better.
This is where shallow teaching about faithfulness collapses.
If someone tells you that obeying God always produces immediate comfort, Joseph's story stands against that claim.
Joseph obeyed.
Joseph suffered.
And yet Genesis 39:21 says:
“But the LORD was with Joseph, and shewed him mercy.” (KJV)
There it is again.
The LORD was with Joseph.
In the house where he served.
And in the prison where he suffered.
God's presence did not disappear when Joseph's circumstances changed.
The prison was not evidence that Joseph had made the wrong moral choice.
And the delay in his vindication was not evidence that God had forgotten him.
That truth should reach someone who is exhausted from doing the right thing without seeing the outcome they hoped for.
You may be waiting for an apology that has never come.
You may be living with consequences caused by another person's dishonesty.
You may have chosen repentance, only to discover that rebuilding trust takes longer than you imagined.
You may have refused to compromise and watched someone else receive the opportunity you wanted.
Do not confuse delayed justice with divine indifference.
But also do not turn Joseph's eventual rise to power into a guarantee that every faithful Christian will receive wealth, promotion, public vindication, or earthly success.
Joseph's story is a particular account of God's providence within His larger purposes.
Its enduring promise is not that every prison becomes a palace in this lifetime.
Its enduring witness is that God remains sovereign and faithful even when the righteous suffer.
Eventually, Joseph would be brought before Pharaoh, interpret his dreams through God's enabling, and be entrusted with extraordinary responsibility.
Through the events recorded in Genesis 41–50, God used Joseph to preserve many lives during famine, including the family through whom His covenant purposes would continue.
Years later, Joseph spoke to the brothers who had betrayed him.
And Genesis 50:20 gives us one of Scripture's clearest testimonies to God's providence:
“But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good.” (KJV)
Notice what Joseph did not say.
He did not call their evil good.
He did not excuse their betrayal.
He did not pretend that injustice was harmless.
He acknowledged their evil intentions while recognizing God's power to accomplish good through circumstances that human beings had wickedly created.
That is not the same as saying God approves of evil.
It is saying evil does not overthrow His sovereign purposes.
And now we come to the most important part of this entire story.
Because if we stop with Joseph, we may leave thinking Christianity is simply about becoming strong enough to resist temptation.
Be disciplined.
Be courageous.
Run away.
Never fail.
But what happens to the person who already failed?
What happens to the husband who crossed the line?
The wife who concealed the relationship?
The unmarried believer trapped in a cycle of sexual compromise?
The Christian who knows the language of holiness but has been hiding a divided life?
What happens when the garment has already been left behind, the boundary has already been crossed, and the conscience is crying out?
Joseph's example can expose our sin.
But Joseph cannot save us from it.
We need someone greater.
We need Jesus.
Joseph was a faithful servant who resisted a particular temptation.
Jesus Christ is the sinless Son of God who resisted temptation and fulfilled the Father's will completely.
Hebrews 4:15 says Jesus was tempted in every respect as we are, “yet without sin.” (KJV)
The Greek expression is:
χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας
Chōris hamartias.
“Without sin.”
Not without understanding human weakness.
Not without experiencing genuine temptation.
Without sin.
Where we have compromised, Jesus remained obedient.
Where we have hidden, Jesus walked in truth.
Where we have betrayed, Jesus remained faithful.
And unlike Joseph, whose suffering was part of God's providential preservation of lives during famine, Jesus' suffering accomplished redemption through His death and resurrection.
He did not merely show us how to escape temptation.
He came to save sinners.
He bore our sins on the cross.
He rose from the dead.
And He calls us to repent, believe the Gospel, and follow Him.
“For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God.” — 1 Peter 3:18 (KJV)
The just for the unjust.
Think about that.
The One who never committed adultery gave Himself for people who have.
The One who never entertained sinful lust came to redeem those enslaved by it.
The One who never lied offered mercy to liars.
The One who never betrayed the Father willingly suffered to reconcile rebellious people to God.
That is the scandal of grace.
Not that sin was insignificant.
But that the sinless Savior paid an immeasurable price to redeem sinners.
And this grace is not a license to return comfortably to the darkness.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's saving grace trains us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions.
Real grace does not merely comfort us while we cling to sin.
It teaches us to turn from sin toward the One who loves us.
And perhaps that is where this article becomes painfully personal.
Because you might be reading it while protecting something you already know needs to end.
A conversation.
A relationship.
A secret habit.
An arrangement built on deception.
A pattern of behavior you keep promising to stop.
You have prayed about it.
You have cried about it.
You have made promises in the middle of the night.
And yet you keep returning.
Listen carefully.
You do not overcome sin by pretending you are stronger than you are.
You begin by bringing the truth into God's light.
Confess your sin to God.
Stop defending what Scripture condemns.
Take practical steps to remove opportunities for compromise.
Seek appropriate accountability from a mature, trustworthy Christian.
Where you have wronged another person, pursue honest repentance and responsible repair, without demanding instant forgiveness or trust.
If abuse, coercion, or threats are involved, seek safety and qualified help. The call to repentance must never be used to blame victims or pressure anyone to remain in danger.
And when shame tells you that you have gone too far to return to Christ, remember His invitation.
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — John 6:37 (KJV)
That promise is not an invitation to cherish sin.
It is an invitation to come to the Savior.
You do not need to clean yourself up enough to earn the right to approach Him.
You need to come honestly, trusting His mercy and surrendering to His lordship.
First John 1:9 declares that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
And Romans 8:1 proclaims that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
Not because their sins were imaginary.
Not because their past never happened.
But because Jesus Christ has accomplished what guilty sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
That is why the Gospel Warrior message is not merely “Run like Joseph.”
It is also “Return to Jesus.”
Run from what is destroying you.
Run toward the Savior who can redeem you.
And if you have already fallen, do not make your failure your permanent identity.
Repent.
Believe.
Rise to walk in the newness of life Christ gives.
You are not saved by Joseph's courage.
You are saved by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
And the same Lord who forgives His people also calls them to holiness.
Perhaps you are the person who needs to end the secret relationship today.
Perhaps you need to confess something you have concealed.
Perhaps you need to stop treating your spouse's trust as something expendable.
Perhaps you need to acknowledge that your private online habits are shaping your heart in ways you have refused to confront.
Or perhaps you are the person who was betrayed, manipulated, falsely accused, or violated.
Then hear this too.
The sin committed against you is not your shame to carry.
Joseph was not guilty of the offense falsely attributed to him.
And you do not need to accept blame for another person's wrongdoing.
Christ sees the wounded as well as the guilty.
His mercy is not reserved only for those who need forgiveness. He also welcomes those who need healing, protection, justice, and restoration.
Some wounds require time, wise counsel, safety, and the support of trustworthy people.
There is no shame in needing that help.
And there is no biblical requirement to pretend that trust has been restored before it actually has.
Jesus Christ is full of grace and truth.
We need both.
Truth without grace can leave a wounded sinner despairing.
A counterfeit grace without truth can leave a sinner comfortable in bondage.
But the Gospel brings us face to face with a holy Savior who loves sinners enough to call them out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
And that is why this message must not end as something we simply admire.
It must become something we respond to.
And if you have been falsely accused or suffered for doing what is right, your testimony may encourage someone who is quietly wondering whether obedience is worth the cost.
You do not have to expose private wounds to prove your faith.
But your honest testimony may become the encouragement another believer desperately needs.
Think of someone you love who may be standing at a dangerous crossroads.
A married friend struggling with temptation.
A young believer surrounded by sexual pressure.
Someone carrying shame over a past mistake.
Someone who thinks their hidden choices have nothing to do with their relationship with God.
Someone who has done the right thing and is now suffering because of it.
Because the world does not need another generation that merely knows how to quote Joseph.
It needs Christians who take holiness seriously, acknowledge their own need for grace, and point broken people toward Jesus Christ.
And if this ministry has helped you grow closer to Jesus, there is another meaningful way you can participate in the work.
Not because God measures your devotion by the amount you contribute.
And certainly not because the Gospel can be purchased.
Salvation is God's gift through Jesus Christ. It is not for sale.
But Scripture does teach that believers may voluntarily support faithful Gospel ministry.
Galatians 6:6 speaks of sharing good things with those who teach the Word, while 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should come from a willing heart, not reluctance or compulsion.
What matters is that any gift be given freely, responsibly, and with a sincere desire to honor God.
And remember, Gospel Warrior is not only about articles.
These resources are part of our desire to encourage a faith that continues beyond a moment of emotional inspiration.
A faith that studies Scripture.
A faith that learns to pray.
A faith that repents.
A faith that grows in wisdom.
A faith that follows Jesus when nobody is watching.
Our deepest desire is that you belong to Jesus Christ.
Because one day, the products will wear out.
The posts will disappear beneath newer posts.
The numbers, reactions, and statistics will fade from memory.
But the Word of God will remain.
And the question Joseph faced will still matter.
How can I do this great wickedness and sin against God?
Maybe the answer you need today is not another excuse.
Maybe it is a confession.
Maybe it is a decision to leave.
Maybe it is a phone call to someone who can help you break a destructive pattern.
Maybe it is finally bringing your shame to the feet of Jesus.
And maybe, for the first time in a long time, you need to stop asking how close you can get to sin without falling and start asking how closely you can walk with the Savior who died to set you free.
Joseph lost his garment, but he refused to surrender his integrity.
He lost his freedom for a season, but God had not abandoned him.
He was falsely accused, but his story did not end with the accusation.
And his life, for all its suffering and remarkable providence, points us toward a far greater Redeemer.
Jesus Christ was condemned though He was without sin.
He endured the cross.
He rose victorious.
And through Him, sinners can be forgiven, the ashamed can find mercy, and the broken can begin a new life.
Do not leave this message merely impressed by Joseph.
Leave it looking to Jesus.
Because Joseph shows us the beauty of faithfulness under temptation.
But Jesus is the Savior who gives hope to those who have failed.
And whether you are standing before temptation, suffering because you refused it, or grieving because you surrendered to it, the call of the Gospel is still before you.
Turn to Christ.
Trust His mercy.
Obey His Word.
Walk in His light.
The door Joseph ran through led away from temptation; the cross of Jesus opens the way home for everyone who has fallen and turns to Him.
